title: Learning in Public. The First Ten Deliberate Hours of a New Skill
body: This is a first draft, and it says so on purpose. The idea was to learn something new in public and to log it like a ledger. Hour by hour, what was attempted, what failed, what the numbers said. Not the polished version that arrives after the skill is safe, but the version with the eraser marks showing. The skill itself does not matter much; pick your own. What matters is the difference between ten deliberate hours and a hundred casual ones. Casual hours feel like progress because time passes and the thing gets easier. Deliberate hours are different. Each one has a question attached, a small honest test, and a note written at the end. The notes are where the learning actually lives. Hour one through three were pure humiliation, and the log says so. The hands did not know where to be. Every attempt ended in something that worked by accident, which is the worst kind of working, because you cannot repeat an accident on purpose. The note from hour three. Slow down by half, and the error rate dropped by more than half. First real lesson, and it cost almost nothing. Hours four through six were the plateau that claims most learners. Nothing improved measurably for two full sessions. The old instinct says push harder. The log said something else. The errors had changed shape, from clumsy to subtle, which means the fundamentals had landed and the next gain would come from precision, not effort. That reframe alone was worth the whole exercise. Hours seven through ten finally produced the first honest results, and the log caught something no feeling would have. The improvements were coming from the boring parts. Position, rhythm, the setup nobody films. Every flashy attempt in the log is followed by a flat line. Every boring attempt is followed by a small climb. Ten hours in, the pattern is already too consistent to ignore. The deeper result is the log itself. Memory is a flattering editor; it keeps the highlights and deletes the plateaus. The page does not flatter. It shows exactly where the time went and what bought the progress, which turns the next ten hours from a mood into a plan. Everyone documents finished things. Almost nobody documents the middle. If you picked one skill and kept a one line log for ten deliberate hours, what would your own plateau teach you?
